summary:
Shin Saimdang (1504–1551) was a Joseon-era Korean artist, calligrapher, writer, and poet, and the mother of Confucian scholar Yi I. Born in Gangneung, she received an unusually broad education for a woman of her time, including literature, history, calligraphy, embroidery, and painting. Her family circumstances and her husband’s consent allowed her to continue developing her artistic skills after marriage.

Saimdang had eight children and was praised for paintings of flowers, insects, landscapes, and other subjects. About 40 of her paintings survive. Her poems include works expressing devotion to her mother. Her children also showed artistic talent, including her daughter Yi Mae-chang and son Yi U.

Remembered as a model of Confucian virtue and called Eojin, or “Wise Mother,” Saimdang has also been criticized by feminist commentators for a legacy that emphasizes women’s family roles. In 2009, she became the first woman depicted on a South Korean banknote, appearing on the 50,000-won note.
